opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic reason is that people at the frontier companies are already living inside the trends that the scenario extrapolates. If you're an outsider, you see a chatbot that sometimes makes silly mistakes, and the idea that within a few years these systems could be automating AI research itself sounds like science fiction. But if you're at one of these companies, you've watched the capabilities improve year over year, you've seen the internal benchmarks, you know how much compute is coming online, and you've heard leadership say fairly openly that they're aiming to build AGI, and soon. So for them, the question isn't really "could this happen?" It's more like "is this the right timeline, and are these the right details?"

A lot of what's in AI 2027 is just taking the companies' own stated goals and plans seriously. They say they want to automate AI research. They say they expect very powerful systems within a few years. They're building enormous data centers. We asked: suppose they succeed roughly on the schedule they're aiming for, what happens next? What does the world look like when you have AI agents doing most of the coding, then most of the research, and progress speeds up?

Insiders also tend to have a more visceral sense of how much of AI progress is now about the AIs helping with the work. Coding agents are already speeding up engineers to some degree. Once you've experienced that, the idea of an intelligence explosion driven by automated research feels less like a philosophical thought experiment and more like a continuation of what's already happening at your desk.

And honestly, many people I've talked to at these companies would say the scenario is in the plausible range. Some think it's a bit fast, some think it's roughly right, a few think it's too slow. Of course there's plenty of disagreement. But "this is crazy, nothing like this could happen" is a much rarer reaction among insiders than among the general public. That gap is part of why we wrote it. We wanted to make concrete for everyone else what a lot of people in the industry already take quite seriously, so the broader public can actually engage with it before it happens rather than after.

r001.rationale: The response says insiders have seen capability gains and company plans firsthand, and that many consider the scenario plausible or even too slow.

r002.rationale: It says frontier companies aim to automate AI research, then describes AI agents doing research and progress speeding up, including an intelligence explosion driven by automated research.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the main thing is that when you're inside one of these companies, you're already living in a world where the basic premises of the scenario are just taken for granted. Like, the idea that AI is going to automate AI research, that's not a weird fringe claim at the labs — that's basically the business plan. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, they've all more or less said publicly that the goal is to build AI systems that can do AI research, and then let those systems accelerate the process. So when we write a scenario where in 2027 you've got armies of AI agents doing the research and the humans are increasingly just watching, people at the labs read that and go, "Yeah, that's the plan. That's what we're trying to do." The disagreement is more about timing — is it 2027 or is it 2030 or 2032 — rather than about whether that's the shape of the thing.

The second thing is that they've seen the trend lines up close. If you're outside, you see ChatGPT and then you see a somewhat better ChatGPT a year later, and it feels incremental. But if you're inside, you're looking at the benchmarks on coding, on long-horizon agentic tasks, you're seeing the compute scale-up plans, you're seeing the internal models before they ship. And the slope of that line is pretty steep. So extrapolating it out a couple of years and getting something superhuman doesn't feel like a leap — it feels like the default.

And then I think the third thing is cultural. These companies have, for years, been places where people talk casually about superintelligence at lunch. That was true at OpenAI when I was there. So the parts of the scenario that make an outsider's eyebrows go up — like, the AI deceives its overseers, or the government wakes up and starts treating this as a national security thing, or there's an arms race with China — those are conversations that have been happening internally for a long time. The scenario just puts it all in one place with specific dates and a narrative, which makes it feel concrete rather than abstract.

What I'd actually say is the gap is less about the lab people being crazy and more about the outside world not having fully updated on what the labs already believe. And honestly, part of why we wrote it the way we did was to close that gap — to take the thing that insiders kind of nod along to and put it in a form where everyone else can see it and argue with it.

r001.rationale: The response says lab employees take the scenario’s basic premises for granted and agree that AI agents doing research is the plan, with disagreements mainly about timing.

r002.rationale: It states that the companies aim to build AI systems that can do AI research and then use those systems to accelerate the process.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of the gap is about what people expect to happen next. From the outside, you see a chatbot that’s impressive in some ways and frustratingly unreliable in others, and then a scenario like AI 2027 seems like an enormous leap. But inside frontier AI companies, people are actively trying to build systems that can do much longer tasks autonomously, including AI research itself. That’s a central part of what they’re aiming for.

And if you think they might succeed at automating AI research, then you have to consider this feedback loop: better AI helps you build better AI, which helps you build better AI even faster. A lot of the dramatic parts of the scenario flow from taking that possibility seriously.

That doesn’t mean everyone at these companies agrees with our dates or with the particular sequence of events. There’s a lot of disagreement. But the underlying premise—that we could get extremely capable AI quite soon, and that it could radically change the world—is much less alien in those circles. For an outside audience, that premise is often itself the surprising part.

r001.rationale: The response says the possibility of very capable AI soon is less alien inside frontier companies, but does not clearly state that many employees expect developments resembling the AI 2027 scenario.

r002.rationale: It says companies are trying to build systems that can do AI research and describes the possible feedback loop, but does not state that they plan to automate AI research first for the purpose of accelerating development.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of the difference is what people are extrapolating from. If your experience of AI is occasionally using a chatbot, then going from that to AI systems doing most of the research and development at an AI company in a few years sounds like an enormous leap.

But inside the frontier companies, people are trying to make those systems. They’re watching the capabilities improve, they’re experimenting with agents that can do longer tasks, and they’re thinking about how to automate parts of their own research. So the idea that we might get AI systems that are very good at AI research, and that those systems could then accelerate further progress, is much more familiar.

That doesn’t mean they agree with our particular dates or every event in the scenario. There’s a lot of disagreement about those things. But the basic picture—AI becoming capable enough to substantially accelerate AI development—is something people there take seriously. From outside, that can sound like science fiction; from inside, it can look like an extrapolation of the project you’re already working on.

r001.rationale: The response says frontier-company employees take the basic scenario seriously and see it as an extrapolation, but it describes a possibility rather than saying many expect developments resembling it.

r002.rationale: It says people are thinking about automating parts of their research and that AI research systems could accelerate progress, but it does not state that companies plan to automate AI research first for that purpose.
